bull_bear.body:
- Scale and integration: fourteen sugar mills, six distilleries and fourteen co-generation plants — 136,000 TCD crushing, 800 KL/D distillery and 449 MW co-generation — placing it "among India's largest integrated sugar and ethanol producers" (Chairman's letter)
- Processes nearly 12% of Uttar Pradesh's sugarcane (Chairman's letter)
- Distillery capacity of 800 KL/D described as "among the largest in the country", enabling participation in India's ethanol blending programme
- Farmer base: trust of over five lakh sugarcane farmers (Chairman's letter)
- Part of the Bajaj Group, described in the Corporate Governance Report as having an established reputation of honesty, integrity and sound governance since inception; Bajaj Group revenues stated at USD 2.0 billion with an asset base of USD 5.3 billion (director profile of Mr. Kushagra Bajaj)
- Captive power from bagasse covers most plant power needs, with surplus sold to the UP state grid
- Restructured capital structure after implementation of the RBI-Prudential-Framework Resolution Plan, with conversion of liabilities into equity instruments and a significantly improved repayment profile substantially reducing near-term debt-servicing obligations (Chairman's letter / Board's Report)
- Nearly a century of operating history (94th Annual Report; incorporated 24/11/1931)
- Institutional sugar franchise being built on FSSC 22000 certification at four units, with named buyers including Pepsi (Varun Beverages), Wrigley, Walmart, ITC, Dabur, Hamdard, Reliance and Udaan (provenance: MD&A, sibling risks_esg bundle)
- Stated absence of import competition: 'Since Sugar imports are not viable and not happening there is no competition from Imported Sugar' (provenance: MD&A, sibling risks_esg bundle)
- COUNTER-EVIDENCE on scale, recorded for balance: BHSL's net sugar production fell from 1.94 million MT in 2019-20 to 1.03 million MT in 2025-26 (estimate), and its share of UP production slipped from 15.35% to 11.48% and of All-India production from 7.08% to 3.71% over the same span (MD&A Table 9, sibling risks_esg bundle)
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Cane availability, cane variety and recovery (raw material risk) — MD&A 'Key risks and concerns' item 1: in Uttar Pradesh the cane variety issue has had 'serious implications on cane yield and sugar recovery in last 2-3 years'. Cane is the single input (BRSR: sugarcane is about 90% of total inputs, sourced from local farmers), so yield/recovery loss feeds straight through to sugar, ethanol and cogen volumes. Mitigation stated is continual investment in cane quality promotion and variety development. A second, self-inflicted leg is flagged explicitly: 'the ability to make timely cane price payments to farmers which is affecting the availability of cane to Group' — cane dues are both a liquidity and a supply problem.
- Sugar price risk — administered cane cost against market-determined sugar realisation, with MSP frozen since 2019 — MD&A item 2: cane prices are fixed by the state government while sugar realisations are wholly market-driven, which 'at times led to a complete mismatch'. The Minimum Selling Price of Rs 31.0 per kg was fixed in February 2019 and has not been raised in the seven years since, while cane FRP rose 29.5%; industry associations are lobbying for Rs 40-42 per kg and for MSP to be indexed to cane price. Management states MSP increase 'is urgently required to prevent sugar price fall during sugar surplus situations / during peak of crushing season'.
- Regulatory and policy dependence — MD&A item 3: 'The biggest risk to the business is the disjointed sugarcane price fixed by the state government', alongside environmental, raw-material-pricing and general policy risk. The offsetting factor stated is continuing Central and State policy and subsidy support to enable mills to pay the fixed cane price — i.e. viability depends on policy decisions (export quotas, ethanol allocations, diversion permissions, subsidy release) rather than on the Company's own actions. The Board's Report separately cites 'non-settlement of subsidy claims under the Sugar Promotion Policy of Uttar Pradesh government' as a cause of the cash-flow mismatch (provenance: sibling capex_expansion / strategy_outlook bundles).
- Ethanol economics — unviable B-heavy/syrup prices and inadequate offtake leaving distillery capacity idle — The de-risking strategy is explicitly not working at current prices: although diversion of sugar to ethanol via B-heavy molasses/sugar syrup began in Sugar Year 2020-21, 'as current Ethanol prices from B Heavy and Syrup Ethanol are not viable, we kept not diverted any sugar towards Ethanol during last 2 years'. Ethanol prices from the sugar route have not been raised for three years and the industry received only 61.1% of its bid quantity in the 2025-26 cycle-I tender (provenance for the tender and price detail: sibling strategy_outlook / capex_expansion bundles). This strands a large part of the 800 KL/day distillery platform.
- Single-state, single-crop geographic and asset concentration — All 14 plants are located in Uttar Pradesh with zero international plants or offices (BRSR item 18), the Company processes nearly 12% of UP's sugarcane, and there are no direct exports (BRSR item 19 prints '-' for number of international countries served — a stated nil, with refined sugar reaching export markets only indirectly via merchant exporters against a Government-issued quota). A UP-specific weather, cane-disease, variety or state-policy shock hits the entire asset base at once. Market share is also eroding: BHSL net sugar production fell to 1.03 million MT (2025-26 estimate) from 1.94 million MT in 2019-20, and its share of UP production slipped from 15.35% (2019-20) to 11.48% (2025-26E) and of All-India from 7.08% to 3.71%.
- Balance-sheet stress and dependence on the lender Resolution Plan — The Company entered a restructuring under the RBI Prudential Framework after a prolonged mismatch between cane procurement cost and flat sugar realisations left it unable to service principal and interest; two of the eight board seats are lender nominee directors (Punjab National Bank and State Bank of India). Continued compliance depends on a Rs 1,000 crore promoter/Company infusion, a minimum Rs 150 crore of non-core asset sales within two years, and a Bajaj Energy shortfall guarantee for any EBITDA/capex shortfall until FY2032 — with security including promoter personal guarantee and pledges of 31,87,43,422 promoter shares (provenance: sibling strategy_outlook bundle; the restructuring text was not routed into this risks bundle). Loss-making subsidiaries (notably Phenil Sugars Limited, which recorded a loss after tax in both FY2025-26 and FY2024-25 — figures deliberately not reproduced) add to the drag.
- Climate change and water security — BRSR material-issue table rows 1 and 2, both classed as Risks with negative financial implications. Climate: 'Variations in rainfall patterns, temperatures, and extreme weather events directly affect crop yields and quality', plus regulatory and reputational risk from rising GHG emissions; mitigated by climate-resilient crop varieties, efficient irrigation and alternative energy. Water: sugar manufacture is water-intensive and 'water scarcity and pollution can profoundly impact the company's functioning, leading to disruptions in the supply chain and increased operational costs'; mitigated by Zero Liquid Discharge across distilleries and reuse of treated sugar effluent.
- Workforce health and safety in a labour-intensive operation — BRSR material-issue row 7 (Risk, negative): the workforce faces occupational hazards including falls, transportation-related incidents, equipment malfunctions and heat stress, and 'non-compliance with safety standards can lead to significant regulatory penalties, reputational damage, and the potential loss of skilled labour'. The Company employs 7,146 people as at March 31, 2026, of whom 4,241 workers are other-than-permanent — a largely seasonal, contract workforce. Mitigation is HIRA and JSA risk assessment, regular safety inspections, third-party and internal cross-functional audits and safety training.
- Channel concentration in sugar sales — Sales are routed overwhelmingly through a small dealer/distributor set: 86.37% of total sales went to dealers/distributors in FY2025-26 (82.11% in FY2024-25) across just 34 dealers (29 prior year), with the top 10 accounting for 71.42% of dealer sales (68.86% prior year) — a structural counterparty concentration even though the AR does not label it a risk (provenance: BRSR Principle 1 'Openness of business' table, routed into the sibling capex_expansion bundle, not into this one). Institutional demand is being built with named buyers including Pepsi (Varun Beverages), Wrigley, Walmart, ITC, Dabur, Hamdard, Reliance and Udaan, supported by FSSC 22000 licences at four units.
- Competition and product-quality migration — Beyond UP, the Company competes with mills in Maharashtra, Karnataka, Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, and in the neighbouring markets of Punjab, Haryana and Bihar with local mills. 'Sugar sales market reach / penetration is purely based on the price parity and Quality with competing mills' — and an increasing number of mills are converting from sulphitation sugar to refined sugar, giving better-quality producers an edge on colour (ICUMSA), grain size and lustre. Offsetting stated fact: 'Since Sugar imports are not viable and not happening there is no competition from Imported Sugar' — a stated absence of import competition.
- Land use, labour rights and ethical-conduct exposure — BRSR material-issue rows 3, 4 and 5, all classed as Risks with negative financial implications: sugar production's substantial land footprint can contribute to deforestation, land degradation and biodiversity loss with reputational and regulatory consequences; labour practices and supply-chain management carry risk of labour-rights violations and substandard working conditions; and corruption or bribery would damage reputation and create legal risk. Mitigations stated are agroforestry and reforestation, biodiversity collaboration, strengthened labour policies with audits and grievance mechanisms, and anti-corruption policies with partner due diligence and ethics training.
bull_bear.title: Bear — key risks

business.body: The Company manufactures sugar, industrial alcohol/ethanol and bagasse-based power from sugarcane crushed at its fourteen Uttar Pradesh plants, selling sugar through mill-wise and area-wise agents to household and institutional buyers, alcohol/ethanol to oil marketing companies for petrol blending, to industrial chemical/paint/ink users and to liquor companies, and surplus power to the Uttar Pradesh state grid while using most generation captively. The BRSR states business activity mix as Sugar 87.37%, Industrial Alcohol 10.23% and power based on bagasse 2.40% of turnover; bagasse is also sold to industrial units for paper and eco-ply board. The Chairman describes an intent to transform the Company from a sugar company with distillery operations into an integrated bio-energy and biorefinery enterprise.
business.title: What they do

business.body:
- **Sugar:** Sugar (including refined sugar), C-molasses
- **Distillery:** Industrial Alcohol, Ethanol (C-heavy molasses route), ENA
- **Power (co-generation):** Bagasse-based power (captive + surplus sold to UP state grid)
- **By-products:** Bagasse (sold to paper and eco-ply board units)

business.title: Competitive strengths

outlook.body:
- Transform the Company from a sugar company with distillery operations into an integrated bio-energy and biorefinery enterprise that maximises value from every part of the sugarcane crop, positioning it at the centre of India's energy transition.
- Scale ethanol production through multi-feedstock flexibility and capacity investment, leveraging the 800 KL/D installed distillery capacity described as among the largest in the country.
- Pursue cost-efficient solutions such as steam saving modules, flex-fuel, Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) and Iso-butanol as the next generation of the Company's green fuel portfolio.
- Rebuild cane availability through farmer support, timely cane payments and investment in high-yield variety development; accelerate cane payments as the financial position strengthens.
- Maintain financial discipline: further strengthen the balance sheet, improve capacity utilisation and drive operational efficiency.
- Deepen ESG commitments — zero liquid discharge, energy conservation and community impact across the 14 plant regions.
- Leverage integrated scale (fourteen sugar mills, six distilleries, fourteen co-generation plants; nearly 12% of Uttar Pradesh's sugarcane processed) with greater operational efficiency, financial discipline and technology-led innovation.
- Complete and operate under the Resolution Plan agreed with the Consortium of Lenders under the RBI Prudential Framework — restructuring of outstanding debt, conversion of liabilities into equity shares and CCPS, and a significantly improved repayment profile that substantially reduces near-term debt servicing obligations; a Framework Agreement was executed on March 26, 2026 between the Company and Lenders.
- Divest identified non-core assets through the Assets Sale Committee — Indonesian coal mines held by PT Batu Bumi Persada and PT Jangkar Prima (under Bajaj Hindusthan (Singapore) Pte Ltd), the Falcon aircraft owned by the Company, shares of the Company owned by BHL Securities Trust, assets of the Company's Ecotec Division, assets of Phenil Sugars Limited, and any other assets decided by the ASC.
- Subsidiary Bajaj Power Generation Private Limited, whose existing power project could not take off in time for reasons beyond the Company's control, is exploring opportunities in the renewable energy sector and will seek necessary regulatory approvals going forward.
- Dividend philosophy: the Board adopted a Dividend Distribution Policy on February 13, 2017 under Regulation 43A of SEBI (LODR), annexed to the Board's Report as Annexure I. The policy's stated intent is to specify the external and internal factors, including financial parameters, considered when declaring dividend, the circumstances in which shareholders may or may not expect dividend, and how retained earnings are to be utilised. It expressly does NOT apply to dividend on preference shares (governed by the terms of issue approved by shareholders), to bonus issues, or to buyback of securities, and it is not a substitute for the Board's annual dividend decision made after considering all relevant circumstances. TRUNCATION: the policy text routed here is cut off at the heading 'Financial Parameters and Interna[l]', so the actual list of parameters and the retained-earnings utilisation clause are missing from this bundle. In practice, for FY2025-26 the Board decided not to recommend any dividend (previous year: nil, and the Shareholder Information section adds 'In view of inadequacy of profit during the year under review'; no dividend has been declared after 2011-12) and decided not to transfer any amount to Reserves. Capital allocation during the year was dominated by the RBI-Prudential-Framework Resolution Plan with the Consortium of Lenders: conversion of YTM/RoR obligations into equity shares and 0.01% Series A CCPS, a Rs 1,000 crore promoter/Company infusion required in FY2025-26, a minimum Rs 150 crore of non-core asset sales within two years of implementation, and lender nominee directors from Punjab National Bank and State Bank of India on the Board (detail in the sibling strategy_outlook bundle). NOT EXTRACTED: Form AOC-1 Part 'A' (subsidiary share capital, other equity, total assets, total liabilities, investments, turnover, PBT, tax, PAT) for both March 31, 2026 and March 31, 2025 appears in this bundle in full, and BRSR item 24 states turnover and paid-up capital; none of those statement figures has been reproduced, per the rule barring primary financial statements.
- Zero Liquid Discharge is implemented across the Company's distilleries, allowing water reuse; treated sugar effluent is used for horticulture, ferti-irrigation and moistening the cane yard, stated as the mitigation for water-scarcity risk (BRSR material-issue table).
- Energy and emission management is the single material issue classified as an OPPORTUNITY with POSITIVE financial implications: carbon-rich by-products bagasse and slop are used as renewable fuels in captive power generation, reducing reliance on fossil energy, with continued focus on cleaner technologies, process optimisation and increased use of alternative fuels; 'Energy conservation and GHG reduction remain integral to BHSL's sustainability agenda.'
- Climate adaptation programme: investment in climate-resilient crop varieties, efficient irrigation techniques and exploration of alternative energy sources to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
- Land and biodiversity: agroforestry practices, reforestation of degraded areas, biodiversity conservation, collaboration with environmental organisations, adherence to land-use regulations and promotion of sustainable land management.
- Safety management system: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment (HIRA) and Job Safety Analysis (JSA), regular safety inspections, periodic audits by third-party experts and internal cross-functional teams, plus recurring training and skill development to strengthen safety culture.
- Labour rights: strengthened labour policies, regular audits, worker-rights training, robust grievance mechanisms, fair wages and prioritised safe working conditions across the supply chain.
- Ethics/anti-corruption: robust anti-corruption policies, due diligence on business partners, regular employee training on ethical conduct, compliance monitoring and community engagement (Code of Conduct for Directors and Senior Management, Code of Fair Disclosure of UPSI, and Vigil Mechanism Policy binding on directors, employees, vendors, suppliers and distributors).
- Governance of ESG: policies cover all nine NGRBC principles (P1-P9), all Board-approved, published at https://www.bajajhindusthan.com/investorcorner-policies.php — twelve policies listed including the Risk Management Policy, Policy on Vigil Mechanism, Policy on Materiality and Dealing with Related Party Transactions, Succession Plan for Board and Senior Management, Board Performance Evaluation and Familiarisation Programme for Independent Directors.
- BRSR is reported on a STANDALONE basis only (not consolidated), and NO external assurance was obtained — 'Name of assurance provider: Not applicable for this financial year; Type of assurance obtained: Not applicable'.
- CSR under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013 is stated as NOT APPLICABLE to the Company.
- Grievance record for FY2025-26: 4 shareholder complaints filed and 0 pending at year-end (2 filed, 0 pending in FY2024-25); a stated NIL — zero complaints filed and zero pending — from communities, investors other than shareholders, employees and workers, customers, value chain partners and 'other', in both years. Zero disciplinary actions against directors, KMPs, employees or workers for bribery/corruption and zero conflict-of-interest complaints in both years (provenance for the anti-corruption and conflict-of-interest counts: BRSR Principle 1, routed into the sibling capex_expansion bundle).
- Workforce composition as at March 31, 2026: 1,722 permanent employees plus 76 other-than-permanent (1,798 total) and 1,107 permanent workers plus 4,241 other-than-permanent (5,348 total); the HR section states a total workforce of 7,146. Gender representation is very low — 8 female employees (0.44%) and 1 female worker (0.02%), 1 woman on the 8-member Board (12.50%) and 0 women among 3 KMPs (0.00%). Differently abled: 5 permanent employees and 18 workers (7 permanent, 11 other-than-permanent).
- Attrition (turnover rate) for permanent employees improved to 9.41% in FY2025-26 from 12.28% in FY2024-25 and 14.29% in FY2023-24; for permanent workers it rose to 8.43% from 7.43% and 7.67%.
- Human resources / industrial relations: a stable and positive industrial relations environment was maintained across all units and the Head Office, with HR initiatives aligned to the 'Group Vision - Think Tomorrow'; a six-month training calendar was scheduled in lean operational periods with average attendance of 28-32 employees per session, delivered by a mix of external experts and in-house faculty, covering electrical safety, fire safety, LOTO, work permit systems, hazard awareness, and ZLD, air pollution control and water conservation (the training-content detail is from the sibling capex_expansion bundle's BRSR extract).
- Food-safety certification: Food Safety System Certification (FSSC) 22000 licences held at four sugar units — Kinauni, Gangnauli, Barkhera and Kundarkhi — supporting the push into institutional sales.
- Sustainable sourcing: 90% of inputs are sourced sustainably, sugarcane being about 90% of total inputs and predominantly bought from local farmers, reflecting reliance on the regional agricultural base (provenance: BRSR Principle 2, sibling capex_expansion bundle).
- Stated GAP: R&D and capital expenditure invested in technologies specifically improving environmental and social impacts was 0.00% of total R&D and 0.00% of total capex in both FY2025-26 and FY2024-25 — a stated nil, not an unknown (provenance: BRSR Principle 2, sibling capex_expansion bundle). End-of-life reclaim processes for plastics/packaging, e-waste, hazardous waste and other waste are all answered 'NA'.
- Chairman's forward ESG commitment: 'Deepening our ESG commitments, zero liquid discharge, energy conservation, and community impact across our 14 plant regions' (provenance: Chairman's letter, sibling profile/strategy bundles).
- Sexual Harassment (POSH) disclosure for FY2025-26: complaints filed Nil, disposed Nil, pending at year-end Nil (provenance: sibling profile bundle's Corporate Governance / Shareholder Information extract).
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: The routed text discloses NO new company capex project with a commissioning or ramp timeline. Capacity is described as already installed and unchanged: fourteen sugar plants with aggregate crushing capacity of 1,36,000 TCD, six distilleries with aggregate industrial-alcohol capacity of 800 kilolitres per day, and fourteen co-generation plants with total power generation capacity of 449 MW (Board's Report, year ended March 31, 2026). The MD&A section 'BAJAJ HINDUSTHAN SUGAR'S (BHSL) POSITION' repeats 14 sugar plants at 136000 TCD and 6 distilleries at 800 KL/day but states 'about 151 MW of surplus power' — a different metric from the 449 MW total co-generation capacity given in the Board's Report and the Chairman's letter; both are recorded separately below rather than reconciled. The 14 mills are evenly spread across Uttar Pradesh — 5 in Western UP (48,000 TCD), 5 in Central UP (48,000 TCD) and 4 in Eastern UP (40,000 TCD) — with named Central-UP mills Barkhera, Maqsoodapur, Gola, Palia and Khambarkhera appearing only in the market-coverage prose; no per-mill capacity is printed. (Back-fill from the sibling profile bundle's BRSR Section A: all 14 plants are located in Uttar Pradesh and there are 3 offices — Mumbai, Noida and Lucknow; that BRSR table was not routed into this capex bundle.) Forward capacity intent is limited to the Chairman's imperatives: scaling ethanol production 'through multi-feedstock flexibility and capacity investment' and pursuing steam saving modules, flex-fuel, SAF and Iso-butanol opportunities — no project, size, cost or date attached. The MD&A de-risking paragraph states 'we are rapidly de-risking our business with the investment in power generation capacity', again without a project or timeline, and adds that although B-heavy/syrup diversion to ethanol began in Sugar Year 2020-21, current B-heavy and syrup ethanol prices are unviable so the Company 'kept not diverted any sugar towards Ethanol during last 2 years'. Cane development is described as a continuing investment ('continually investing in cane variety development', 'major thrust of the group on cane development'). Industry-level expansion context supplied in the MD&A (not company projects): oil companies' September-2021 dedicated-ethanol-plant scheme offering guaranteed lifting for time-bound new distilleries; ethanol movement by rail rakes/pipeline started at Mathura, Panipat and Kanpur depots; eased tender conditions (security/penalty cut from 5% to 1% from ethanol year 2020-21, then raised from 1% to 3% since ethanol year 2022-23); OMC payment cycle down to ~30 days from 35-40 days with a stated expectation of 21 days; and 20% ethanol blending with 95 RON becoming a mandatory norm for petrol nationwide with effect from 1st April 2026. BRSR Principle 2 records a STATED NIL: R&D 0.00% and Capex 0.00% of total R&D/capex invested in specific technologies to improve environmental and social impacts, in both the current and previous financial year. The block is reproduced verbatim: '[page 303] Year ended | As at / Estimated amount of contracts remaining to be executed on capital account and not provided for (net of advances). / 0.24 / 8.01'. outlook.body:
- Indian sugar output has fallen for two consecutive years (2024-25 and 2025-26) on weather-related issues in Maharashtra and Karnataka and cane-variety issues in Uttar Pradesh; in these two years gross production exceeded consumption but net production (after diversion to ethanol) was below consumption.
- Industry-wide, management flags lower cane availability, underutilisation of sugar plant capacity, lower sugar recovery, no increase in sugar MSP, no increase in ethanol prices and non-availability of adequate ethanol orders resulting in underutilisation of distillery capacity.
- All-India gross sugar production peaked at 39.0 million mt in 2021-22 and has declined continuously since; 2024-25 gross was a five-year low 29.6 million mt (net 26.1 million mt); 2025-26 gross is estimated at 30.9 million mt (+4.4%) with net production around 27.8 million mt, far below the initial 34-35 million mt estimates (a 10%+ deviation from ISMA's initial 34.3 million mt estimate).
- Closing sugar stocks for 2025-26 are estimated at an all-time low 4.1 million mt, 14.6% of domestic consumption, easing inventory carrying cost and quality-deterioration burden; despite low stocks the report notes adequate market availability and no abnormal price surge.
- Exports remain restricted to Government quotas: nil quota in 2023-24, 1.0 million mt in 2024-25, and 2.0 million mt for 2025-26 (1.5 million mt pro-rata to all mills plus 0.5 million mt to willing mills) — but only about 0.7 million mt is estimated to actually be exported, on five-year-low international prices and logistics bottlenecks from the Middle East conflict; major exports were low-quality white (sulphitation) sugar helped by a strong USD and regional FOB premiums.
- Sugar MSP has been unchanged at Rs 3,100 per qtl since 2019 while cane FRP rose 29.5% from Rs 275 to Rs 365 per qtl (10.25% recovery basis) for 2026-27 and UP SAP (early variety) rose 23.1% from Rs 325 to Rs 400 per qtl; sugar prices continue to prevail below production costs and fall to alarmingly low levels during the crushing season. Media reports suggest the Government was considering an MSP increase to Rs 3,800 per qtl, but a favourable decision is awaited; the industry is also seeking automatic indexation of MSP to cane price.
- Ethanol economics are the key margin swing factor: 2025-26 is the third consecutive year without a Government price increase for B-heavy and sugar-syrup based ethanol, making current ethanol prices unviable against cost, so many mills — particularly in UP — are prioritising sugar production and keeping ethanol capacity idle.
- Ethanol allocation shortfall: in 2025-26 cycle-I the industry received orders for 288.5 crore litres through the sugar route against bids of 472 crore litres (61.1%), versus 311.9 crore litres against 391.3 crore bid (79.7%) in 2024-25 cycle-I, after which no further tender cycle was floated for B-heavy/syrup ethanol — a clear case of oversupply and surplus distillation capacity.
- Demand-side policy levers management points to: raising blending beyond 20%, flexi-fuel vehicles taking E85/E100, ethanol cooking stoves, ethanol blending with diesel, and Sustainable Aviation Fuel — supported by import-substitution and forex-savings arguments amid the Middle East conflict.
- Weather outlook: 2026 is estimated to be an El-Nino year with monsoon below normal at 90-95% of Long Period Average, which may affect the 2026-27 crop and also sowing for the 2027-28 season; however, since 2024 and 2025 were normal monsoon years there is no indication of a production shortfall for 2026-27.
- USDA estimates a 12% increase in Indian sugar production (raw value) from 30.0 million mt to 33.6 million mt in 2026-27; other analysts peg 2026-27 higher by 1.0-1.5 million mt versus last year.
- World sugar balance (ISO, updated Feb 2026, Oct-Sept year): 2025-26 production 181.29 million mt against consumption 180.07 million mt — a surplus of 1.22 million mt versus a deficit of 3.46 million mt in 2024-25; end stocks 93.30 million mt and stocks/consumption 51.81%.
- For 2026-27 third-party views diverge: Green Pool raised its global deficit estimate to 4.30 million mt from 1.66 million mt citing a shift to higher ethanol production at the expense of sugar, while Covrig Analytics cut its surplus estimate to 800,000 MT from 1.4 million mt.
- Brazil Centre-South (UNICA, April-March): 2025-26 cane crush fell 1.7% to 611.15 million mt while sugar production rose 0.6% to 40.43 million mt on higher diversion to sugar (average 50.38%, having run up to 54% in the first half before weak sugar prices and better ethanol parity pulled it down); ethanol production 33.72 billion litres and TRS 137.79; diversion of cane towards sugar is estimated to come down during 2026-27.
- Thailand (USDA): sugar production rose almost 10% to 11.26 million mt in 2025/26 and is estimated to fall 15.6% to 9.50 million mt, with exports easing to 6.0 million mt from 7.0 million mt (the narrative dates this decline as '2025-2026' while the table places the 9.50/6.00 figures under the 2026-2027 column — the mismatch is reproduced as printed).
- Crude oil (Brent) — a major macro driver of sugar prices and of Brazilian cane diversion to ethanol — opened at USD 74.49/bbl on 1 April 2025, touched a low of USD 58.92/bbl in December 2025 and stood at USD 118.35/bbl on 31 March 2026, with extreme volatility from February 2026 on the start of the Middle East conflict.
- Currency: the Brazilian real moved from 5.68 in early April 2025 to a high of 6.01, a low of 5.13 in February 2026, closing at 5.18; the Indian rupee depreciated 9.2% from 85.6 to 93.5 per USD (strongest 84.3, weakest 94.8) — the chart narrative labels this period '2024-25' while quoting 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026 dates.
- Company-level tailwinds cited by the Chairman: continued improvements in ethanol realisations, healthier sugar inventories and strengthening industry fundamentals reinforce the attractiveness of the integrated business model; the restructured capital structure substantially reduces near-term debt servicing obligations.
- Structural remedies management calls for: better cane varieties, use of Artificial Intelligence for improved cane productivity, and water conservation mechanisms such as drip irrigation, rainwater harvesting, trash shedding and mulching to address volatility in sugar production, declining productivity and recovery, cane varietal issues and weather vagaries.
- No company-level order book is disclosed. The only order/allocation pipeline discussed is industry-wide ethanol tendering: in 2025-26 cycle-I the industry received orders for 288.5 crore litres of ethanol through the sugar route against bids of 472 crore litres (61.1% of bid quantity); in 2024-25 cycle-I, orders of 311.9 crore litres were placed against bids of 391.3 crore litres (79.7%), after which no further tender cycle was floated by the oil companies for B-heavy molasses / syrup ethanol.
- Sugar export entitlement is quota-based rather than order-book based: for 2025-26 the Government allowed a 2.0 million mt export quota (1.5 million mt to all mills in proportion to production plus 0.5 million mt to willing mills), against which only about 0.7 million mt is estimated to be exported.

deepdive.thesis: Bajaj Hindusthan Sugar Limited, founded in 1931 by Shri Jamnalal Bajaj and part of the Bajaj Group, is an integrated sugarcane processor running fourteen sugar mills, six distilleries and fourteen bagasse-based co-generation plants in Uttar Pradesh, described in the report as among India's largest integrated sugar and ethanol producers.

open.horizon: as on March 31, 2026 (tenor of OCDs ongoing)
open.item: The Company paid the first instalment of the Optionally Convertible Debentures issued to lenders; outstanding OCDs as on March 31, 2026 stood at Rs 3,215.31 crore, secured on a first pari-passu basis over all current assets and all movable and immovable fixed assets plus promoter personal guarantee, corporate guarantees and pledges from group/subsidiary companies.

20% ethanol blending with 95% RON becomes a mandatory norm for petrol sold across the country with effect from 1st April 2026, with Flexi Fuel Vehicles taking higher blends in process of launch — a demand driver for the Company's distillery capacity.

Shortfall undertaking by way of corporate guarantee from Bajaj Energy Private Limited for a maximum of up to Rs 300 crore (at a maximum of Rs 150 crore per year) till financial year 2032 — the end of the Specified Period under the RBI Prudential Framework — to meet any cumulative shortfall in EBITDA / funds requirement for capital expenditure under the proposed Resolution Plan.
Scale ethanol production through multi-feedstock flexibility and capacity investment (no project, size, cost or date disclosed).
Pursue cost-efficient solutions such as steam saving modules, flex-fuel, Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) and Iso-butanol as the next generation of the Company's green fuel portfolio.

The Company/industry seeks rationalisation of ethanol prices from the sugar route — current basic prices are Rs 65.61 per litre for sugar-syrup ethanol and Rs 60.73 per litre for B-heavy ethanol, last increased in 2022-23 when cane FRP was Rs 305 per qtl (since up 19.7% to Rs 365 per qtl for Sugar Year 2026-27) — plus opening of ethanol exports and new consumption channels to absorb surplus capacity.
open.promised: 65.61 (syrup) / 60.73 (B-heavy) INR per litre — current basic ethanol prices sought to be raised

open.item: The Company/industry is pursuing an increase in Sugar MSP to a minimum of Rs 42 per kg (industry associations have represented for Rs 40-42 and for linking MSP to cane price), MSP having been unchanged at Rs 31 per kg since February 2019 while FRP rose 29.5% to Rs 365 per qtl for 2026-27.

open.horizon: "in times to come" — no date stated
open.item: Oil-company ethanol payments are now received in about 30 days on average versus 35-40 days earlier, and are expected in time to come down further to 21 days on average.
Continue investing in cane quality promotion and cane variety development to raise yield, recovery and cane availability for the mills.
De-risk the business through investment in power generation capacity, described as non-cyclical and expected to generate steady cash flows year on year (no project or timeline stated).
2026 is estimated to be an El-Nino year with below-normal monsoon at 90-95% of Long Period Average, which may affect the crop in the 2026-27 season and also sowing for the 2027-28 season.

Sugar MSP has been frozen at Rs 3,100 per qtl since 2019 while cane FRP and UP SAP have risen 29.5% and 23.1% respectively, leaving sugar prices below production cost — a mismatch management explicitly flags and is lobbying to have MSP indexed to cane price.
open.promised: 3,100 MSP vs FRP 365 / UP SAP 400 INR per qtl

open.item: Management flags that Government has not increased B-heavy and sugar-syrup ethanol prices for a third consecutive year, making ethanol unviable against cost, with inadequate ethanol orders leading mills — particularly in UP — to prioritise sugar and keep ethanol capacity idle.

Bajaj Power Generation Private Limited is exploring opportunities in the renewable energy sector and will seek necessary regulatory approvals as may be required going forward, its existing power project not having taken off in time.
Pursue cost-efficient solutions like steam saving modules, flex-fuel, SAF and Iso-butanol opportunities as the next generation of the Company's green fuel portfolio.

CCPS issued to lenders carry a buy-back feature, a tenor of up to 20 years and a 0.01% p.a. cumulative coupon/dividend, and will convert into equity shares quarterly on every reduction of lenders' shareholding below 50%, with conversion price computed by a registered valuer per SEBI ICDR Regulations and the RBI Prudential Framework.
open.promised: 0.01% coupon; tenor up to 20 years % p.a. / years

open.horizon: two years from the date of implementation of the Resolution Plan
open.item: Promoters/Company shall arrange a minimum of Rs 150 crore through sale of identified non-core assets within two years from the date of implementation of the Resolution Plan, as identified by the Assets Sale Committee (Indonesian coal mines of PT Batu Bumi Persada and PT Jangkar Prima, the Falcon aircraft, shares held by BHL Securities Trust, Ecotec Division assets, Phenil Sugars Limited assets and any other assets decided by the ASC).
Deepen ESG commitments — zero liquid discharge, energy conservation and community impact across the Company's 14 plant regions.
Maintain financial discipline by further strengthening the balance sheet, improving capacity utilisation and driving operational efficiency.
Rebuild cane availability through farmer support, timely cane payments and investment in high-yield variety development, and accelerate timely cane payments as the financial position strengthens.

risks.note: MD&A 'Key risks and concerns' item 1: in Uttar Pradesh the cane variety issue has had 'serious implications on cane yield and sugar recovery in last 2-3 years'. Cane is the single input (BRSR: sugarcane is about 90% of total inputs, sourced from local farmers), so yield/recovery loss feeds straight through to sugar, ethanol and cogen volumes. Mitigation stated is continual investment in cane quality promotion and variety development. A second, self-inflicted leg is flagged explicitly: 'the ability to make timely cane price payments to farmers which is affecting the availability of cane to Group' — cane dues are both a liquidity and a supply problem.
risks.risk: Cane availability, cane variety and recovery (raw material risk)

risks.note: MD&A item 2: cane prices are fixed by the state government while sugar realisations are wholly market-driven, which 'at times led to a complete mismatch'. The Minimum Selling Price of Rs 31.0 per kg was fixed in February 2019 and has not been raised in the seven years since, while cane FRP rose 29.5%; industry associations are lobbying for Rs 40-42 per kg and for MSP to be indexed to cane price. Management states MSP increase 'is urgently required to prevent sugar price fall during sugar surplus situations / during peak of crushing season'.
risks.risk: Sugar price risk — administered cane cost against market-determined sugar realisation, with MSP frozen since 2019

risks.note: MD&A item 3: 'The biggest risk to the business is the disjointed sugarcane price fixed by the state government', alongside environmental, raw-material-pricing and general policy risk. The offsetting factor stated is continuing Central and State policy and subsidy support to enable mills to pay the fixed cane price — i.e. viability depends on policy decisions (export quotas, ethanol allocations, diversion permissions, subsidy release) rather than on the Company's own actions. The Board's Report separately cites 'non-settlement of subsidy claims under the Sugar Promotion Policy of Uttar Pradesh government' as a cause of the cash-flow mismatch (provenance: sibling capex_expansion / strategy_outlook bundles).

The de-risking strategy is explicitly not working at current prices: although diversion of sugar to ethanol via B-heavy molasses/sugar syrup began in Sugar Year 2020-21, 'as current Ethanol prices from B Heavy and Syrup Ethanol are not viable, we kept not diverted any sugar towards Ethanol during last 2 years'. Ethanol prices from the sugar route have not been raised for three years and the industry received only 61.1% of its bid quantity in the 2025-26 cycle-I tender (provenance for the tender and price detail: sibling strategy_outlook / capex_expansion bundles). This strands a large part of the 800 KL/day distillery platform.
risks.risk: Ethanol economics — unviable B-heavy/syrup prices and inadequate offtake leaving distillery capacity idle

risks.note: All 14 plants are located in Uttar Pradesh with zero international plants or offices (BRSR item 18), the Company processes nearly 12% of UP's sugarcane, and there are no direct exports (BRSR item 19 prints '-' for number of international countries served — a stated nil, with refined sugar reaching export markets only indirectly via merchant exporters against a Government-issued quota). A UP-specific weather, cane-disease, variety or state-policy shock hits the entire asset base at once. Market share is also eroding: BHSL net sugar production fell to 1.03 million MT (2025-26 estimate) from 1.94 million MT in 2019-20, and its share of UP production slipped from 15.35% (2019-20) to 11.48% (2025-26E) and of All-India from 7.08% to 3.71%.
risks.risk: Single-state, single-crop geographic and asset concentration

risks.note: The Company entered a restructuring under the RBI Prudential Framework after a prolonged mismatch between cane procurement cost and flat sugar realisations left it unable to service principal and interest; two of the eight board seats are lender nominee directors (Punjab National Bank and State Bank of India). Continued compliance depends on a Rs 1,000 crore promoter/Company infusion, a minimum Rs 150 crore of non-core asset sales within two years, and a Bajaj Energy shortfall guarantee for any EBITDA/capex shortfall until FY2032 — with security including promoter personal guarantee and pledges of 31,87,43,422 promoter shares (provenance: sibling strategy_outlook bundle; the restructuring text was not routed into this risks bundle). Loss-making subsidiaries (notably Phenil Sugars Limited, which recorded a loss after tax in both FY2025-26 and FY2024-25 — figures deliberately not reproduced) add to the drag.
risks.risk: Balance-sheet stress and dependence on the lender Resolution Plan

risks.note: BRSR material-issue table rows 1 and 2, both classed as Risks with negative financial implications. Climate: 'Variations in rainfall patterns, temperatures, and extreme weather events directly affect crop yields and quality', plus regulatory and reputational risk from rising GHG emissions; mitigated by climate-resilient crop varieties, efficient irrigation and alternative energy. Water: sugar manufacture is water-intensive and 'water scarcity and pollution can profoundly impact the company's functioning, leading to disruptions in the supply chain and increased operational costs'; mitigated by Zero Liquid Discharge across distilleries and reuse of treated sugar effluent.

BRSR material-issue row 7 (Risk, negative): the workforce faces occupational hazards including falls, transportation-related incidents, equipment malfunctions and heat stress, and 'non-compliance with safety standards can lead to significant regulatory penalties, reputational damage, and the potential loss of skilled labour'. The Company employs 7,146 people as at March 31, 2026, of whom 4,241 workers are other-than-permanent — a largely seasonal, contract workforce. Mitigation is HIRA and JSA risk assessment, regular safety inspections, third-party and internal cross-functional audits and safety training.

meta.thesis: Bajaj Hindusthan Sugar Limited, founded in 1931 by Shri Jamnalal Bajaj and part of the Bajaj Group, is an integrated sugarcane processor running fourteen sugar mills, six distilleries and fourteen bagasse-based co-generation plants in Uttar Pradesh, described in the report as among India's largest integrated sugar and ethanol producers.
